segments.text: In this video, we'll be going over the next question about oscillations, and this is a question that I really like because it demonstrates a lot of what we have learned, not only oscillations but also work, and it's a really good application of oscillations as well in part b.
So, what we have here is a simple pendulum consists of a small sphere that hangs from a string with negligible mass.
The top end of the string is fixed. The sphere is pulled to point A so that the string makes an angle theta, and the sphere is released from rest and it oscillates back and forth.
The work done on the sphere by Earth between points A and B is W.
The pendulum is then taken to planet X, and the mass of planet X is the same as the mass of Earth, but the radius is greater than the radius of Earth.

So, first of all, when we see that the mass of planet X is the same as the mass of Earth but the radius is greater, then that means that G on planet X will be smaller than the acceleration of Earth, because the gravitational field strength would be smaller for a greater radius.
And the sphere is then brought back to point A and swung again on planet X, and you have to justify why the work done on planet X is less than the work done on planet E.
Well, as I've said in another video, I don't remember which one, but I've said this before, the work is equal to force times distance.

And also another thing is force times distance cosine theta, but also AP Physics 1 has a formula booklet, and it basically has everything you need to know to solve these questions, other than one or two formulae.
So what you have here is work is equal to force times distance, or force times distance in the direction.
And so it's just mainly about applying these and understanding what you're doing.
So force, well, force, Newton's law, is mass times acceleration. In this case, it's mass times gravity, because that's the acceleration times distance.
And the same thing for X equals force times distance, and it's equal to mass times gravity on X times D, while this is gravity times E on D.
But like I've explained before, since the acceleration on X is lower, so this is lower than that, and M and D are constants in both cases, because the distance and the mass of the ball are the same,
then we can conclude that the work done on X is less than the work done on E, and that's basically what you need to explain.
I'm not going to write it down, but the question is solved. You just need to state what I've said.
Okay, a new pendulum is made by hanging the same small sphere on a different string with negligible mass.
Different string means that the length of the string is different.
The new string is slightly elastic, and the length of the string may increase or decrease depending on the tension applied.
I haven't read this question in a while, but from what I see here, you don't really need to mind this.
All you need to know is that the length of the string can vary.
On Earth, when the sphere is displaced from the vertical and released from rest, the new pendulum oscillates with this period.
And then the new pendulum is taken to a different planet with the same radius, but a larger mass.

And on planet Y, it oscillates with period T Y.
And you have to explain how T Y could be larger than T, or it could also be smaller than T.

So basically, first of all, when we do this, we want to know our variables in play.
And I would be pulling up the formula sheet if I was doing the exam right now.
And you would know that T P equals 2 pi root L over G, as we've learned.
So T equals 2 pi root L over G.
Now, it's kind of obvious now why it could be either larger or smaller.
If the length of the string is way, way larger, then the period on Earth would be greater.
So if it's elastic, if it's more elastic, then the period on Earth could be greater.
But, sorry, the period on planet Y could be greater.
Because if it's more elastic, then the length on planet Y would be larger, because there would be a greater tension force.
But if it's not so elastic, that means that gravity on planet Y would be way, way larger than the gravity on planet E or Earth.
So if it's not so elastic, then the period on planet Y would be less.
And the period on planet E would be greater.
So it really depends on the elasticity of the string.
And that's basically how you answer the question.
So say that gravity is inversely related to period.
So if gravity is greater, then the period will be smaller.
And also say that length is related, or the root of length is related to period.
So if it's really elastic, which means the length will be greater, then the period on planet Y would be greater, because it would have a larger length.
Since it's elastic, and planet Y's greater gravitational field would pull it down more, and result in more elasticity and more length.
And that's basically how you answer this question.
Okay, that's all for today's video, and I hope you enjoyed. Thank you!
